cells.tense: You're standing in the middle of not-knowing and it isn't scaring you off.
cells.ask: Tell one person the next step you're taking while it's still half-formed, and let that be enough of an answer for today.
cells.core: You can sit with a question that doesn't have a shape yet and still move. Most people need the whole road before they take a single step. You take the step and let the road show up as you go, and you've gotten used to that being how it works.\n\nThe cost is that carrying an open question without closing it early gets tiring in a way that's easy to miss. Feed it anyway. Say the half-formed thing out loud to someone today. Naming where you're headed, even roughly, tells you whether the direction is actually yours or just the one that came easiest.
cells.sheetLine: You move before the road is visible, and that's the skill.
cells.verb: sensing what isn't here yet and moving toward it before the shape is clear
cells.place: the part of a life that moves without a map

cells.tense: You're already living in the version where this works out, and the present keeps interrupting.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're imagining and do the smallest real version of it today — the version a camera could catch.
cells.core: You're running ahead of what's actually here. The future keeps getting written before the present has arrived, and you're living in the draft. There's real insight in that — you can see connections other people miss — but the picturing has outrun the making.\n\nWhen you try to force the picture into being, you skip the part where it has to grow at its own speed. That's what's exhausting you: pushing something that isn't ready to be pushed, and calling the exhaustion proof you care enough. Try the opposite. Take one piece of what you're seeing and do a small real version of it — something that could actually happen today, with what's on hand. Let the rest stay in draft.
cells.sheetLine: You've outrun your own vision and now you're chasing it.

cells.tense: There was a moment you trusted the not-knowing, and you haven't gone back to it.
cells.ask: Say one true thing you've noticed but haven't said yet — out loud, to no one in particular, and let it stand.
cells.core: You stopped moving before you could see clearly. The road stopped revealing itself and you stopped walking it. What's still there, even if it doesn't feel like it, is the ability to notice something true without needing to prove it first. That ability didn't go anywhere. It just hasn't been used.\n\nDon't try to imagine your way out of this. Smaller than that. Say one thing you've seen — not a theory, not a plan, just something you've actually noticed — and let it be said without defending it. That's the muscle that's gone quiet, and it comes back by using it, not by waiting to feel ready.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped trusting what you noticed, and that's the thing to get back.

cells.tense: You're already navigating the uncertainty — you're just calling it something else.
cells.ask: Name one thing you decided recently without admitting it was a decision, and say the deciding was yours.
cells.core: You're already moving through this without a map. The choices are being made — which way to lean, what to try next, what to let go of — and you're doing it without saying out loud that you're the one moving. But you're the one moving. The steering is happening; your name just isn't on it yet.\n\nThat matters because when you don't own the call, you can't learn from it. You can't tell whether the direction is right if you didn't say you picked it. Start with one thing. Name a decision you made recently — out loud — and say it was yours. Not a big declaration, just an honest one.
cells.sheetLine: The steering is yours. Say so.
